name: Ensulizole

lead: Ensulizole is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs mostly UVB light. Because it dissolves in water, it appears in light lotions and daily facial moisturisers with SPF, so people can wear sun protection every day under makeup and slow sun-driven aging.

It absorbs UVB in the skin-surface layer of a product and offers little UVA protection. It is an approved US over-the-counter sunscreen active, and published research on ensulizole alone is thin, with most covering sunscreens generally.

paras: It is used in daily facial moisturisers and lotions with SPF, usually combined with filters such as avobenzone, zinc oxide or bemotrizinol for UVA coverage.

Sunscreen filters as a group can cause allergic or photoallergic reactions in some people, and labels advise stopping use if rash or irritation occurs. Environmental studies have detected PBSA in water and examined effects on fish and mussels.

web.title: Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun (FDA)

angle.text: Ensulizole gives light daily facial sun protection, so there is less photoaging and uneven tone over time. Evidence is sunscreen-class, and it needs other filters for UVA coverage.

lead: Ensulizole, also known as phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid (PBSA) and 2-phenylbenzimidazole-5-sulfonic acid, is a water-soluble organic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreens and daily facial moisturisers. It helps people look better over the long run by shielding skin from UV, and the FDA says sunscreens help prevent sunburn and, used with other sun-protective measures, reduce early skin aging caused by the sun.[1] Its cosmetic appeal is that it dissolves in water, so it can go into light, non-greasy lotions and gels that people are willing to wear on the face every day.[2]

Chemically it is a benzimidazole sulfonic acid. It is primarily a UVB absorber (UVB is 280 to 315 nm) with minimal UVA coverage (315 to 400 nm), so it is generally paired with other filters when broad-spectrum protection is intended: avobenzone, bemotrizinol, titanium dioxide or zinc oxide in the United States, and ecamsule or bisoctrizole elsewhere.[2] In the United States it is a monograph (over-the-counter) sunscreen active, and the FDA required its name, ensulizole, on US sunscreen labels from 1999.[2][3]

Published human research on ensulizole specifically is limited. The literature includes in vitro efficacy comparisons, photoallergy clinic series, a registered sun-protection formulation trial, and environmental studies that detect it in water; sunscreens as a class have a much larger body of research.[4][5][6][7][8][9]

paras: Ensulizole is used in sunscreens, moisturisers with SPF and cosmetics as a UVB absorber. It absorbs mainly in the UVB range (280-315 nm), and in the United States it is typically paired with avobenzone, bemotrizinol, titanium dioxide or zinc oxide for UVA coverage.[2] Outside the US it may be combined with UVA filters such as ecamsule or bisoctrizole.[2]
US drug labels list it alongside other actives, for example with octisalate and zinc oxide in a body sunscreen whose label states it helps prevent sunburn.[3]

The free acid is poorly water-soluble, so formulators use soluble salts of the compound. Because it dissolves in the water phase, ensulizole lets a sunscreen feel lighter and less greasy than oil-phase filters alone, which is why it shows up in lotions, gels and daily facial moisturisers.[2]

sections.h: What SPF and UVB filters do
paras: The FDA explains that SPF is measured mainly against UVB, so it mostly reflects UVB protection; broad-spectrum products protect against both UVA and UVB.[1] Because ensulizole is chiefly a UVB absorber, products that rely on it for protection are combined with UVA filters to achieve a broad-spectrum label.[2][1] The FDA states that sunscreens help prevent sunburn and reduce risks of skin cancer and early skin aging caused by the sun, and that they should be used together with other protective measures; products that are not broad spectrum or have SPF below 15 carry a warning that they only help prevent sunburn.[1]

An in vitro comparison of 18 EU-authorised filters at their maximum permitted concentrations ranked the sun protection factor each produced in a topical product. Phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid scored 8.31 on that scale, above octyltriazone (7.80) and below octyl dimethyl PABA (8.71), octocrylene (10.41) and octyl methoxycinnamate (10.42), with the highest values for diethylhexylbutamidotriazone, isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate and anisotriazine.[4] The authors calibrated the method against in vivo results by adjusting the applied mass of product.[4]

A 2012 laboratory study tested 21 EU-authorised UV filters in a mouse ear-swelling model and reported that 13 showed significant anti-inflammatory effects, including phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid with 78 percent oedema inhibition; the authors suggested this could affect the in vivo SPF value.[10]
A registered Phase 3 trial (n=10, 2009) evaluated the sun protection of sunscreen formulas, though the registry entry alone does not establish effect sizes for ensulizole.[5]

Sunscreen chemicals as a group are recognised causes of allergic and photoallergic contact dermatitis. A 15-year clinic review of 402 patients with suspected photosensitivity found that 80 (20 percent) had allergic or photoallergic reactions to one or more UV absorbers; among the 10 absorbers tested after 1989, phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid produced 1 allergic and 7 photoallergic reactions, far fewer than isopropyldibenzoylmethane (30 allergic, 32 photoallergic) or methylbenzylidene camphor.[6]

In a Swedish photopatch series of 355 patients, 7.9 percent had allergic reactions to tested sunscreen allergens, mostly benzophenone-3; the authors reported two cases of photocontact allergy to phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid (Eusolex 232), which they said had not been reported previously.[7]
US labelling for products containing ensulizole advises external use only, avoiding broken skin, keeping out of eyes, and stopping use if irritation or rash occurs.[3]

Because it is water-soluble and used widely, PBSA is detected in wastewater and surface water, and appears in studies of sorption to sewage sludge.[8][11] In Czech surface waters PBSA reached up to 13 micrograms per litre, higher than benzophenone-3 or benzophenone-4; in a chronic toxicity test, rainbow trout exposed to PBSA for 21 and 42 days had raised tissue concentrations and increased activity of certain cytochrome P450 enzymes, while no pathological changes were evident in liver or gonads.[9] A 2021 study used biomarkers to assess sublethal effects of ensulizole and octocrylene in the marine mussel Mytilus edulis.[12]

Wikipedia lists ensulizole among sunscreening agents approved by one or more agencies, including the US FDA, the EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration.[2] In 1999 the FDA required the name ensulizole to appear on US sunscreen labels.[2]

No clinical trial has examined ensulizole on its own for a cosmetic or appearance outcome. The only registered human study found is a small Phase 3 sun-protection formulation test.[5] Broader human data come from photopatch-testing series of sunscreen allergens as a group, which included phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid among their test substances.[6][7] Laboratory work includes the in vitro SPF ranking and the mouse anti-inflammatory screen described above.[4][10]
